pages.x: In 138 BC the Han emperor Wu sent an officer, Zhang Qian, west to look for allies against the Xiongnu, horse nomads who raided China. The Xiongnu caught him and kept him for ten years. He escaped, went on, and came home after thirteen years with news of lands no Chinese had seen.

Zhang Qian told of the tall, fast horses of Ferghana, in Central Asia, said to sweat blood. Emperor Wu wanted them for his cavalry. When Ferghana would not sell, he sent armies thousands of kilometres across the deserts, and in 101 BC they came back with the horses.

With Han forts guarding the oasis towns of the Tarim Basin, camel caravans carried silk, lacquer and iron west and brought back horses, glass, jade, grapes and alfalfa. Few traders went the whole way: goods passed from hand to hand, through Parthian, Kushan and Sogdian merchants.

Romans had no idea how silk was made: some thought it was combed from the leaves of trees. Rich Romans wore it all the same. The writer Seneca grumbled that it hid nothing of a woman's body, and Pliny the Elder that luxuries from the east drained the empire of its gold.
China kept secret for centuries how silk was made: it is spun from the cocoons of silkworms, fed on mulberry leaves.
pages.fx: Around 552, the story goes, two monks smuggled silkworm eggs to Constantinople in hollow canes for the emperor Justinian, and Europe began to make its own silk.

pages.x: Ideas travelled with the goods. Buddhist monks carried their faith from India into China along the trade routes from the first century AD, followed later by Christians, Manichaeans and Muslims. Paper travelled the other way, reaching Samarkand by the 700s and Europe after that.
No one at the time spoke of a Silk Road. A German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, made up the name, Seidenstrasse, in 1877. It was never one road but a web of routes across land and sea.

For more than 1,500 years the Silk Road joined China, India, Persia, the Arab world and Europe, carrying goods, faiths, inventions and also diseases such as the Black Death. It tied the old world together long before ships sailed around it.
